pairs.rationale: Both introduce Jesus' warning in the hearing of the people while addressing His disciples. Matthew names crowds and disciples; Luke says all the people were listening.

Both expose a contradiction between teaching the law and failing to practice it. Matthew tells hearers not to imitate the teachers' works; Paul challenges the teacher with examples of transgression. Romans does not repeat Matthew's instruction to observe what these teachers say.
Both accuse legal teachers of placing burdens hard to carry on others while refusing to touch those burdens with a finger. Matthew addresses scribes and Pharisees; Luke addresses experts in the Law.

This same-book comparison connects the criticism of works performed to be seen by people with Jesus' earlier warning against practicing righteousness for that purpose. Matthew 6:1 does not mention phylacteries or garment fringes.
Both warnings describe love of the foremost synagogue seats and foremost places at dinners, with the order of the two locations reversed.
Both criticize the desire for greetings in the marketplaces. Matthew additionally mentions being called Rabbi; Mark's cited verse instead mentions long robes and does not include the title.

Matthew grounds the instruction about the title Rabbi in the disciples' one Teacher; John records Jesus affirming that they rightly call Him the Teacher and Lord. The shared point is Jesus' teaching authority; John does not repeat Matthew's title restriction or all-brothers statement.

Both appeal to one Father shared by the people addressed. Matthew specifies the heavenly Father and forbids calling someone on earth father; Malachi places the one-Father appeal beside the one Creator and a rebuke of betrayal between brothers. Malachi does not itself contain Matthew's naming prohibition.
Both redefine precedence through service. Matthew says the greatest will be the servant; Mark says one wishing to be first must be last and servant of all.
Both give the reversal that the self-exalting person will be humbled and the self-humbling person exalted. Luke places it after a teaching about seating at a banquet.

Both charge religious teachers with failing to enter and hindering others who would enter. Matthew speaks of shutting the kingdom of the heavens; Luke speaks of taking away the key of knowledge. The two objects are related in the warnings but are not identical wording.

Jesus' earlier teaching rejects oath-taking by sacred or divine-associated objects rather than establishing classes of supposedly binding and nonbinding oaths. This same-book comparison gives the broader oath-teaching background; the earlier passage does not specifically discuss sanctuary gold.

The earlier same-book instruction not to swear at all bears on the disputed distinction between swearing by an altar and swearing by its gift. Its examples are heaven, earth and Jerusalem, not this verse's altar and gift, so it supplies a related principle rather than an exact restatement.

Both attribute sanctifying holiness to the altar. Exodus calls the altar most holy and says everyone touching it will be sanctified, while Matthew specifically speaks of the altar sanctifying a gift. The persons-and-gift difference and the absence of an oath rule in Exodus are retained.

Matthew relates the sanctuary to the One dwelling in it; the psalm says the Lord is in His holy temple and immediately places His throne in heaven. The comparison concerns sacred dwelling and divine presence, without claiming the psalm identifies the same physical sanctuary.

Matthew's identification of heaven as God's throne recalls the Lord's statement that heaven is His throne. Matthew applies that imagery to swearing by heaven; Isaiah is not itself an oath prohibition.

Both rebuke meticulous tithing of herbs while neglecting weightier duties, and say the latter should be done without omitting the former. Matthew names mint, dill and cumin with justice, mercy and faithfulness; Luke names mint, rue and every herb with justice and love of God.
Both address Pharisees who clean the outside of cup and dish while the inside is full of plunder. Matthew adds self-indulgence; Luke adds wickedness.

Both direct attention from the cleaned exterior to the morally disordered interior. Matthew commands cleansing the inside first so the outside becomes clean; Luke connects inner and outer creation and instructs giving what is within as alms. The remedies are compared without being made identical.

Both use tombs to criticize the hearers through concealed uncleanness. Matthew describes whitewashed tombs beautiful outside but full of bones and uncleanness; Luke describes unmarked tombs crossed unknowingly. The distinct tomb images remain visible.

Both contrast favorable appearance before people with an inward condition exposed by God or Jesus. Matthew names hypocrisy and lawlessness within an outwardly righteous appearance; Luke says God knows the hearts of those justifying themselves before people.
Both criticize building the prophets' tombs in the context of the fathers' killing the prophets. Matthew additionally names decorating the righteous people's monuments.

Both discuss the present generation's relation to the fathers who killed the prophets while the descendants build their tombs. Matthew quotes a denial of complicity; Luke records Jesus' charge that their building witnesses to approval. The quoted defense is not attributed to Luke.

Both characterize the hearers as witnesses concerning their fathers' deeds against the prophets. Matthew stresses their identity as sons of the murderers; Luke explicitly charges approval of the deeds. These are related accusations with different formulations.

Matthew's command to fill the fathers' measure can be compared with Genesis' description of the Amorites' sins not yet being filled up. Both use a completion image for accumulated wrongdoing; the peoples and historical situations differ, and Genesis does not name Matthew's hearers.

This same-book comparison repeats the address brood of vipers and the question about escaping coming judgment. John asks about fleeing coming wrath in Matthew 3; Jesus here asks about fleeing the judgment of Gehenna.

Both predict the sending of messengers, some of whom will be killed and persecuted. Matthew has Jesus say I send and names prophets, wise people and scribes; Luke attributes the saying to God's wisdom and names prophets and apostles. Matthew's crucifixion, synagogue flogging and city-to-city details are additional.

Both describe accountability for bloodshed stretching from Abel to Zechariah, killed between altar and sanctuary or house. Matthew calls Zechariah son of Berechiah; Luke gives no father. This link does not resolve the identity by substituting the different patronymic in a separate Chronicles account.
Both assign accountability for the preceding bloodshed to this generation. Matthew says all these things will come upon it; Luke says the blood will be required of it.

Both lament Jerusalem's killing of prophets and stoning of the sent, then compare Jesus' wish to gather its unwilling children with a bird gathering a brood beneath its wings. Matthew specifically says hen and chicks; Luke says bird and brood.
Both announce the house being left to the hearers. Matthew explicitly calls it desolate; that adjective is absent from the supplied Luke verse, which continues with the future greeting.

Jesus quotes the blessing upon the One coming in the Lord's name. The Saints psalm supplies that clause and continues with blessing from the Lord's house; Matthew uses the clause in His statement about seeing Him again. The target is Greek-numbered Psalms 117:26.

Both begin the temple-destruction discourse with Jesus leaving the temple and a disciple or disciples drawing attention to its buildings. Mark adds admiration of the stones and buildings; Matthew gives the disciples' approach without quoting it.
Both predict that the impressive temple buildings will be thrown down with no stone left upon another. Matthew introduces the prediction with Truly I tell you.

Both place a private question on the Mount of Olives about when the predicted events will happen and their sign. Mark names Peter, James, John and Andrew and the temple opposite them; Matthew explicitly asks about Jesus' coming and the age's consummation, which Mark's question does not formulate that way.
Both open Jesus' reply with the warning to see that no one leads the hearers astray.

Both warn that many will come in Jesus' name and deceive many. Matthew gives their claim as I am the Christ, while Mark's supplied wording is I am he; the explicit Christ title is not silently inserted into Mark.
Both tell hearers not to be alarmed by wars and reports of wars because these must happen but the end is not yet.
Both predict nation against nation and kingdom against kingdom, with earthquakes in various places and famines. The order of earthquakes and famines differs.
Both describe the preceding upheavals as the beginning of birth pains. Mark includes the saying in the same verse as the earthquakes and famines.

Both warn of handing over, death and hatred because of Jesus. Mark specifies councils, synagogue beatings, rulers and betrayal within families; Matthew here describes affliction and hatred by all nations. The scope and sequence of the warnings are not treated as identical.

Both predict betrayal of people close to one another. Matthew describes many stumbling, betraying and hating each other; Mark specifically lists brother against brother, father against child and children against parents, without repeating Matthew's whole description.

Both warn of false prophets leading people astray. Mark additionally names false christs, signs and wonders and the attempted deception of the chosen; Matthew develops those features later in this discourse.
Both promise salvation to the one who endures to the end. Mark attaches it to hatred on account of Jesus' name, while Matthew places it after the preceding warnings of betrayal and lawlessness.

Both say the good news must reach all nations. Matthew explicitly makes worldwide proclamation a testimony and says the end then comes; Mark says the proclamation to all nations must happen first without repeating the whole formulation.

Both warn of the abomination of desolation standing in an improper or holy location and include the reader's instruction to understand. Matthew explicitly attributes it to Daniel and calls the place holy; Mark says where it ought not and proceeds directly to flight from Judea.

Daniel's supplied text places an abomination of desolations upon the temple, the distinctive image Jesus identifies as spoken through Daniel. The wording, long time-period description and desolation context are retained as saved; this link does not select a historical identification or recalculate the periods.
Both direct those in Judea to flee to the mountains when the preceding sign appears.
Both prohibit someone on the housetop from going down into the house to collect possessions during the flight.
Both prohibit someone in the field from turning back to take a cloak.
Both pronounce woe on pregnant women and those nursing infants in those days.
Both direct prayer that the crisis or flight not happen in winter. Matthew additionally mentions the Sabbath; that additional qualification is absent from Mark's supplied verse.
Both describe an affliction unparalleled from the world's or creation's beginning until now and never to be repeated. Mark explicitly speaks of the creation God created.
Both say that without shortening the days no flesh would be saved and that the shortening is for the chosen. Mark explicitly names the Lord as shortening the days and calls the chosen those He chose.
Both forbid believing reports that the Christ is here or there.
Both predict false christs and false prophets performing signs and wonders to deceive, if possible, the chosen. Matthew calls the signs great.
Both remind the disciples that Jesus has told them beforehand. Mark also commands vigilance and says He has told all things beforehand.
Both reject directions that locate the awaited figure here or there and tell hearers not to go after such reports. Matthew specifies wilderness and inner rooms; Luke does not name those places.

Both compare the Son of Man's manifestation with lightning lighting the sky. Matthew says from east to west and speaks of His coming; Luke says from one part of the sky to another and speaks of His day.

Both give the image of eagles gathering where the body or corpse is. Matthew says corpse, while Luke says body in answer to a question about where; the comparison does not resolve the saying's full eschatological interpretation.
Both place darkness of sun and moon, falling stars and shaken heavenly powers after the affliction of those days. Matthew explicitly says immediately after.

Both describe the Son of Man coming on clouds with power and great glory. Matthew also includes His heavenly sign and the mourning of all earthly tribes; those additional elements are not supplied by the cited Mark verse.

Matthew's Son of Man coming upon heaven's clouds recalls Daniel's vision of one like a son of man coming upon the clouds of heaven. The supplied Saints Daniel wording and visionary context are retained; this is a comparison of the distinctive cloud imagery rather than a proposed date or a harmonization of every figure in the vision.

Both describe angels gathering the chosen from the four winds and the farthest extents. Matthew adds a great trumpet and speaks of one end of heaven to the other; Mark speaks of earth's end to heaven's end.
Both direct learning from the fig tree, whose tender branch and emerging leaves indicate that summer is near.
Both tell hearers that seeing these events indicates nearness, at the doors. The comparison retains the source's wording without deciding which proposed referent of it is intended.
Both say this generation will not pass away until all these things happen. The link records the shared saying without assigning an interpretive date.
Both contrast passing heaven and earth with Jesus' words that will not pass away.
Both deny knowledge of the day or hour to anyone, including the angels and the Son, and reserve it to the Father. Matthew specifies angels of the heavens and the Father alone.
Both compare the days of Noah with the coming or days of the Son of Man. The phrasing differs between Matthew's coming and Luke's days.
Both describe ordinary eating, drinking and marriage continuing until the day Noah entered the ark. Luke includes the ensuing flood in the same verse.

Both portray the flood bringing a decisive end to the people outside the ark, as part of the Son of Man comparison. Matthew explicitly says they did not know until it came; Luke says the flood destroyed them all without that separate statement of unawareness.

Both picture two people together with one taken and the other left. Matthew locates the pair in a field, while Luke places two in one bed at night; these differing settings are not harmonized or replaced by an absent Luke field verse.
Both describe two women grinding together with one taken and one left.
Both require watchfulness because the master's or Lord's coming is not known. Matthew asks about the day of your Lord's coming; Mark uses the household master's return and lists watches of the night.
Both use a householder who would have prevented a break-in if he had known when the thief was coming. Matthew explicitly adds keeping watch and specifies the watch of the night; Luke uses hour.
Both command readiness because the Son of Man comes at an unexpected hour.
Both ask who is the faithful and prudent servant appointed by the master to distribute household food at the proper time. Luke calls him a steward and specifies the food allowance.
Both bless the servant whose returning master finds him carrying out that responsibility.
Both promise that the faithful servant will be appointed over all the master's belongings.
Both introduce the servant's inward claim that his master is delaying. Luke continues directly into the abusive conduct described in Matthew's next verse.

Both describe the servant beating fellow servants and indulging in eating and drinking or drunkenness during the presumed delay. Luke specifically names male and female servants; Matthew mentions dining with drunkards.
Both warn that the master will return on a day the servant does not expect and at an hour he does not know.

Both describe the master cutting the unfaithful servant in two and assigning his portion with an excluded group. Matthew names hypocrites and adds weeping and grinding of teeth; Luke names the unfaithful or unbelievers and does not include that final formula.

deferred.reason: The specific statement about scribes and Pharisees occupying Moses' chair was read. General instructions to heed legal authorities do not establish this particular chair or its attribution to these groups; no sufficiently precise target was retained.

The prohibition on being called guides, grounded in the one Guide, the Christ, was read. Broad passages about teachers or shepherds were not treated as direct counterparts to this distinct instruction.

The indictment of travel to make a proselyte and then making him twice a son of Gehenna was read. No sufficiently precise separate passage for this distinctive conversion-and-corruption claim was established.

The sanctuary's sanctifying the gold and the resulting ranking of sanctuary over gold were read. General consecration rules were not retained as though they explicitly establish this particular relationship or the disputed oath distinction.

The inference that swearing by the altar includes everything upon it was read. Related altar-holiness rules do not themselves state this oath's scope; no sufficiently specific independent target was retained.

The distinctive gnat-straining and camel-swallowing image was read. Other images of disproportionate moral attention were considered too general to serve as a close separate counterpart in this initial review.

The prediction that increasing lawlessness will make many people's love grow cold was read. Broader lists of wrongdoing or apostasy do not repeat this causal connection, and no sufficiently specific target was retained.

review_notes: Read every one of the 89 actual Matthew 23–24 source units in the pinned Saints English record. Matthew 23:14 is absent from that record and was not invented or imported.
Retained targets were read in the exact pinned Saints originals, preserving the edition's divisions, original verse-ID gaps and Greek-based numbering. Every target range follows saved original order.
The prophets-blood comparison preserves Matthew's Zechariah son of Berechiah and Luke's lack of a patronymic; no substitution of Zechariah son of Jehoiada is made.

Differences are explicit for herbs and neglected duties, the tomb images, desolate in Matthew but absent in Luke's house notice, heavenly-body imagery, the excluded servant groups, and the field-versus-bed pair.
Psalms 117:26, Psalms 10:4, Exodus 29:37, Daniel 9:27 and 7:13 retain their actual Saints wording and numbering. Exodus refers to persons touching the altar, distinct from Matthew's gift.

Same-book comparisons are identified as internal teaching links, not independent historical confirmation. Daniel and eschatological parallels do not assign fulfillment dates or resolve disputed identifications.
Deferrals receive no completed-source or pair credit. The numerical hourly target does not justify adding generic matches.
Source wording, display text, continuations, anchors and IDs are unchanged; these are AI-assisted English passage comparisons, with independent specialist review still pending.
